parakeet: Owners are taught to give without question even when they struggle because God sees your sacrifice. Leaders continue to grow in influence and wealth while the needs of the people go unmet. When you put these moments together from the wealthy gifts at birth to the offerings during life to the rich man's tomb at death, a consistent pattern emerges. Jesus, as portrayed in the gospel narratives, receives. He accepts sacrifice. He is served by the poor and supported by the rich, but we never see him redistribute wealth, organize community economics, or materially liberate anyone. He offers miracles on conditions. He praises giving, but never gives materially. He critiques power, but doesn't model alternative structures. This isn't just about Jesus. It's about the system that has been built in his image. A system where poverty is praised, leaders are untouchable, and the faithful are expected to give until it hurts while calling it holy. It's time we stopped spiritualizing the suffering of the poor and started asking where all the money went. This isn't a hit piece. It's an honest inquiry. If we're going to use Jesus as a model for justice, love, and service to the poor, we need to look closely at the narrative, not just the spin. Maybe Jesus was a man with a dream, a mission, maybe even a man with the message. But maybe, just maybe, he was also a man who knew how to build loyalty by asking people to give him everything without giving anything back. The poor will always be with you, is what he said. But why? If your miracles were meant to liberate them, why would they always be poor? Rather than modeling a movement that empowered the poor, the gospel narratives often present an ideology where the poor are instruments of virtue signaling, sacrificial loyalty and miracle dependency, not recipients of structural change.
